mainTopic: Why the Torah needs 'בעל השור נקי' if 'men, not oxen' already exempts an ox owner from דמי ולדות, and רבי עקיבא's reading about דמי עבד
overview: This amud opens by finishing two pictures of how רבי אליעזר answered רבי עקיבא. In one picture he is a fisherman who keeps every fish, so both his answers stand. In רב טביומי's version, in the name of רבא, he drops the first 'הֵמִית' answer once he finds a better one. The גמרא then brings a ברייתא where רבי יוסי הגלילי reads 'בעל השור נקי' as freeing the owner from דמי ולדות. רבי עקיבא objects that the miscarriage פסוק already says 'men, not oxen', and the גמרא agrees that this is a strong point. רב עולא and then רבא each try to show why the פסוק is still needed. רב עולא's answer is rejected because it would make a תם stricter than a מועד, and אביי knocks down רבא's answer by applying the same logic to בושת. אביי and רבא then explain that the difference is about whether the woman was harmed. רב אדא בר אהבה says it is really about whom the attackers meant to hit, and רב חגי brings a ברייתא that supports him. Finally, another ברייתא quotes רבי עקיבא, who reads 'בעל השור נקי' as freeing the owner from דמי עבד.

steps.title: The fisherman who keeps every fish
steps.stepSummary: This ends the first version's analogy. Even after his strong answer, רבי אליעזר added a weaker one too, like a fisherman who takes big fish and small fish alike.
steps.simpleTranslation: He finds big ones, he takes them; small ones, he takes them too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a picture that explains why רבי אליעזר added a second, weaker answer. A fisherman keeps every fish he catches, big or small.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, רבי אליעזר's first answer was already the better one. He still added a weaker answer as an extra, just as a fisherman does not throw away small fish. So both answers stay on the table.

keyTerms.meaning: He finds
Big ones
Small ones
Takes

phrases.english: He finds big ones – he takes them,
small ones – he takes them too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the first version's explanation of why רבי אליעזר gave two answers.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He added the weaker answer even after the stronger one, the way a fisherman keeps both big and small fish.

steps.title: The fisherman who throws back the small fish
steps.stepSummary: רב טביומי, in the name of רבא, says רבי אליעזר gave the 'הֵמִית' answer first. When he thought of a better answer, he dropped the first, like a fisherman who throws back small fish once he finds big ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב טביומי said in the name of רבא: He first told him 'killed.' This is like a fisherman pulling fish from the sea. When he finds small ones, he takes them. When he finds big ones, he throws away the small ones and takes the big ones.
steps.whatsHappening: A different אמורא reverses the order of רבי אליעזר's two answers. The weaker 'הֵמִית' answer came first and was later replaced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, both answers stand. Here, the first answer ('הֵמִית', about an ox that killed) was a temporary placeholder. Once the better answer came, the first was thrown away, so only the second answer counts.

keyTerms.meaning: Killed; the label for the answer about an ox that killed
At first
A fisherman pulling fish out of the water
Throws away

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two fishermen. In the first version he keeps everything. In רב טביומי's version he throws back the small fish, so the first answer is dropped.

phrases.english: Rav Tavyumei said in the name of Rava:
He said 'killed' to him first –
phrases.notes: 'Killed' is a nickname for רבי אליעזר's answer about an ox that killed, from earlier in the sugya.

phrases.aramaic: מָשָׁל לְצַיָּיד שֶׁשּׁוֹלֶה דָּגִים מִן הַיָּם,
phrases.english: it is like a fisherman pulling fish from the sea,
when he finds small ones – he takes them,
when he finds big ones – he throws away the small ones
and takes the big ones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite order of רבי אליעזר's answers from the first version.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'הֵמִית' answer came first and was replaced by the better answer.

steps.title: רבי יוסי הגלילי: the owner is free from paying for the unborn children
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא brings רבי יוסי הגלילי's reading of 'בעל השור נקי': the owner is free from paying דמי ולדות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches about 'The owner of the ox shall be clear.' רבי יוסי הגלילי says: clear from paying for the miscarried children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new ברייתא with another explanation of the words 'בעל השור נקי'. רבי יוסי הגלילי says they mean the owner does not pay דמי ולדות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, the sugya explained 'נקי' in other ways. Here, רבי יוסי הגלילי says it means that if an ox causes a woman to miscarry, the owner is not liable for the unborn children. This sets up רבי עקיבא's objection in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner of the ox shall be clear (שמות 21:28)
Payment for unborn children lost in a miscarriage

phrases.english: It is taught in another baraita: 'The owner of the ox shall be clear' –
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says:
clear from paying for the offspring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא with another reading of 'בעל השור נקי'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'נקי' teaches that the ox's owner does not pay דמי ולדות.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: the פסוק already says 'men', not oxen
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא objects that a different פסוק already teaches this. The verse about miscarriage says 'men', so oxen are not included.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to him: But the Torah says, 'When men fight and hurt a woman.' It says men, not oxen.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא challenges רבי יוסי הגלילי. We do not need 'נקי' to teach this, because the miscarriage פסוק already speaks only about men.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The miscarriage law (שמות 21:22) says 'אנשים', men. That already shows an ox's owner does not pay דמי ולדות. So רבי יוסי הגלילי's reading makes 'נקי' teach something we already know.

keyTerms.meaning: But it says; introduces a פסוק used as a challenge
When men fight (שמות 21:22)
And they strike or hurt
And not oxen

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the rule that only a person, not an animal's owner, pays דמי ולדות. The sugya will need to explain what 'נקי' teaches instead.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said to him: But it says:
'When men fight and hurt a woman' –
men, and not oxen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוסי הגלילי's reading from the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי הגלילי's reading that 'נקי' means freedom from דמי ולדות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Redundancy: the word 'אנשים' in the miscarriage פסוק already leaves out oxen, so 'נקי' cannot be needed for this.

steps.title: The גמרא agrees that רבי עקיבא's objection is strong
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רבי עקיבא's objection makes good sense. This puts pressure on רבי יוסי הגלילי to explain why he needs 'בעל השור נקי'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says רבי עקיבא's challenge is a good one. This sets up the next move: someone now has to defend רבי יוסי הגלילי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא said the miscarriage פסוק says 'men', so oxen are already excluded. If so, 'בעל השור נקי' seems to have nothing left to teach about דמי ולדות. By agreeing with him, the גמרא is quietly asking how רבי יוסי הגלילי would answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Well, nicely, correctly
He is saying

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva is speaking well!
phrases.notes: This is the גמרא hinting at a question: so what would רבי יוסי הגלילי answer him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Agrees with רבי עקיבא's objection from Step 4, which now needs an answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוסי הגלילי's reading of 'בעל השור נקי' as an exemption from דמי ולדות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'אנשים' in the miscarriage פסוק already excludes oxen, so 'בעל השור נקי' would teach nothing new.

steps.title: רב עולא: without the verse, a תם ox might have been liable
steps.stepSummary: רב עולא בריה דרב אידי says the פסוק is needed. Without it, we might have said that 'men' excludes only oxen that are like men, which are מועד. Then a תם ox would pay. 'בעל השור נקי' teaches that it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עולא the son of רב אידי said: The verse was necessary. You might have thought: 'Men' excludes only oxen that are like men. Just as men are always considered forewarned (מועד), so too only forewarned oxen are excluded. A תם ox would then be liable. So the Torah wrote 'the owner of the ox is clear' to teach that it is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב עולא defends רבי יוסי הגלילי. He shows that 'אנשים' alone could have left a תם ox liable, so 'בעל השור נקי' is needed to exempt it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person is always treated as מועד, fully responsible for what he does. So 'men, not oxen' might have excluded only oxen that are like men, meaning מועד oxen. That would leave a תם ox paying דמי ולדות, and 'בעל השור נקי' comes to exempt the תם too.

keyTerms.meaning: It was necessary (the verse is not extra)
You might have thought (introduces a mistaken assumption)
A forewarned ox with a pattern of goring, whose owner pays full damages
An ox with no pattern of goring, whose owner pays only half damages
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב עוּלָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Ulla the son of Rav Idi said:
It was necessary,
since it would enter your mind to say:
'Men' – but not oxen that are similar to men;
phrases.notes: 'Men' is the word from the miscarriage פסוק, שמות 21:22.

phrases.aramaic: מָה אֲנָשִׁים מוּעָדִין – אַף שְׁוָורִים מוּעָדִין,
phrases.english: just as men are forewarned, so too forewarned oxen are excluded,
but a תם ox would be liable;
so the Merciful One wrote 'the owner of the ox is clear' – that he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection that Step 5 endorsed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the verse is needed by pointing out a mistake we would have made without it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'אנשים' excludes only מועד oxen, so a תם ox would pay דמי ולדות.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'בעל השור נקי' exempts a תם ox from דמי ולדות as well.

steps.title: רבא: that makes the weaker case stricter
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects רב עולא's answer. A מועד is the more serious case, so it makes no sense to exempt the מועד while making the תם pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The native is on the ground and the stranger is in the highest heavens?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רב עולא's answer with a saying about a native who sits low while a stranger sits high.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מועד ox is always treated more strictly than a תם ox. Under רב עולא's mistaken assumption, the מועד would be exempt while the תם paid, which turns everything upside down. Nobody would ever think that, so the פסוק is not needed to prevent it.

keyTerms.meaning: A native, someone who belongs (here, the stricter מועד)
A stranger or newcomer (here, the more lenient תם)
The highest heavens

phrases.english: Rava said:
The native is on the ground,
phrases.notes: The 'native' stands for the מועד, which should be treated at least as strictly as the תם, yet here it ends up exempt.

phrases.english: and the stranger is in the highest heavens?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב עולא's answer from Step 6.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The entire mistaken assumption that רב עולא proposed
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It makes a תם stricter than a מועד, which no one would ever think, so no פסוק is needed to rule it out.

steps.title: רבא's answer: the verse exempts only a תם, so a מועד pays
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a new answer. Without the פסוק we would have exempted מועד oxen, and a תם all the more so. 'בעל השור נקי' teaches that only a תם is exempt, while a מועד pays דמי ולדות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: The verse was necessary. You might have thought: 'Men' excludes oxen that are like men. Just as men are forewarned, so too forewarned oxen are excluded, and a תם ox would be exempt by a קל וחומר. Then the Torah wrote 'the owner of the ox is clear' to teach that a תם is exempt but a מועד is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא replaces רב עולא's answer. In his version, 'בעל השור נקי' limits the exemption to a תם, so a מועד ox does pay דמי ולדות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the פסוק, 'אנשים' would exclude מועד oxen, and a קל וחומר would exempt a תם too, so no ox would ever pay. By saying 'נקי' specifically about the תם ox, the Torah shows that only a תם is exempt. That makes a מועד ox liable, which keeps the normal order where a מועד is stricter.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (introduces a replacement answer)
An 'all the more so' argument; here, if even the stricter מועד is exempt, the more lenient תם surely is
Then, afterward

steps.whatToRemember: Under רבא's answer for רבי יוסי הגלילי, 'בעל השור נקי' means a תם ox is exempt from דמי ולדות, but a מועד ox is liable. אביי challenges this answer in the next two steps.
steps.confusionAlert: Both answers start with the same words. The difference is the mistaken first thought. רב עולא says we would have made the תם liable. רבא says we would have exempted every ox, so the פסוק comes to make the מועד pay.
steps.whyThisMatters: This makes רבי יוסי הגלילי's reading work without breaking the rule that a מועד is always stricter than a תם.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
It was necessary,
since it would enter your mind to say:
'Men' – but not oxen that are similar to men;

phrases.aramaic: מָה אֲנָשִׁים מוּעָדִין – אַף שְׁוָורִים מוּעָדִין,
phrases.english: just as men are forewarned, so too forewarned oxen are excluded,
and all the more so, תם oxen are exempt;
then the Merciful One wrote 'the owner of the ox is clear' –
a תם is exempt, but a מועד is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: אִיצְטְרִיךְ, סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב עולא's answer, which Step 7 rejected, with a new answer to רבי עקיבא's objection.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the exemption: the verse narrows it to a תם instead of adding it
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every ox, תם and מועד alike, would be exempt from דמי ולדות.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a תם ox is exempt from דמי ולדות, and a מועד ox is liable.

steps.title: אביי applies רבא's method to humiliation
steps.stepSummary: אביי argues that if רבא's reasoning works for דמי ולדות, it should work the same way for בושת. That would lead to the strange result that a מועד ox's owner pays בושת.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: But if so, let us say the same about humiliation: 'Men', and not oxen that are like men. Just as men are forewarned, so too forewarned oxen are exempt, and innocuous ones all the more so. Then the Torah wrote 'the owner of the ox shall be clear', meaning only an innocuous ox is exempt, and a forewarned one is liable!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבא's answer from Step 8. He shows that the same line of reasoning would also apply to the laws of בושת (humiliation).
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse about בושת also talks about 'men' fighting. So by רבא's logic we would first exempt even a מועד ox from בושת, and a תם all the more so. Then 'בעל השור נקי' would come and limit the exemption to a תם, so a מועד's owner would pay בושת. אביי is setting up a problem with this result, which he completes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Payment for humiliation or embarrassment
But if that is so (introduces an argument showing where your logic leads)

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
phrases.notes: "Him" is רבא, who gave the answer in Step 8.

phrases.english: But if that is so,
regarding humiliation too, let us say this:
phrases.notes: The בושת verse (דברים 25:11) also begins with "men" fighting, so the same reasoning could be used there.

phrases.english: "Men", and not oxen that are like men;
just as men are forewarned,
so too forewarned oxen are exempt,
and all the more so innocuous ones are exempt;
then the Torah wrote "the owner of the ox shall be clear":
an innocuous ox is exempt, and a forewarned one is liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's answer from Step 8 by applying the same reasoning to בושת.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's explanation that 'בעל השור נקי' teaches that only a תם is exempt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same structure applies to the בושת verse, so a מועד's owner would have to pay בושת. The next step shows why that result is a problem.

steps.title: If so, the ברייתא should have mentioned humiliation
steps.stepSummary: אביי blocks the possible reply 'yes, that is true.' If it were true, the ברייתא would have said that רבי יוסי הגלילי exempts the ox owner from both דמי ולדות and בושת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that this is indeed so, then the ברייתא should teach: 'The owner of the ox shall be clear': רבי יוסי הגלילי says he is exempt from payment for the offspring and from humiliation!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי closes the escape route. One could accept that רבא's reasoning also covers בושת, but then the ברייתא should have said so, and it did not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא quotes רבי יוסי הגלילי as using 'בעל השור נקי' only for דמי ולדות. If the פסוק also taught a rule about בושת, he would have mentioned both payments. Since the ברייתא mentions only one, רבא's answer is weakened.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (introduces a possible reply)
Let it teach, meaning the ברייתא should have said so
Payment for the unborn babies lost in a miscarriage

steps.whatToRemember: אביי's two-part attack shows that רבא's answer from Step 8 cannot stand, so a new explanation is needed.

phrases.english: And if you say, indeed it is so,
if so, let it teach:
phrases.notes: He means the ברייתא that quotes רבי יוסי הגלילי.

phrases.english: "The owner of the ox shall be clear":
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says:
he is exempt from payment for the offspring and from humiliation!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא הָכִי נָמֵי, אִי הָכִי, לִיתְנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes אביי's challenge by ruling out the reply that a מועד really does pay בושת.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible defense that רבא's reasoning really does apply to בושת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the פסוק taught a rule about בושת, the ברייתא would have mentioned בושת together with דמי ולדות. It mentions only דמי ולדות.

steps.title: New answer: the difference is whether the woman was harmed
steps.stepSummary: אביי and רבא together explain that 'men' teaches that people pay for the babies only when the woman is not killed. Without our פסוק, oxen might have paid even when she was killed, so 'בעל השור נקי' teaches that the ox owner is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי and רבא both say: 'Men': if there is no harm to the woman, they are punished; if there is harm to the woman, they are not punished. But not oxen, which are punished even though there is harm. Then the Torah wrote 'the owner of the ox shall be clear', meaning he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops רבא's earlier answer and gives a new one in the name of both אביי and רבא. It explains what 'men' would have taught us about oxen and why 'בעל השור נקי' is still needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People pay דמי ולדות only when there is no אסון. When the woman dies, they face a death penalty instead of paying. From 'men' we might have learned that oxen are different, so their owners would pay even when there is אסון. 'בעל השור נקי' rules this out and teaches that the ox owner is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Harm or disaster; here, the woman dying
They shall be punished; here it means paying money
Both of them

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'not oxen' does NOT mean oxen pay less. It means oxen might have paid MORE, even when there is אסון. That is exactly why 'בעל השור נקי' is needed to exempt them.

phrases.english: Rather, Abaye and Rava
who both say:
"Men":
if there is no harm to the woman, they shall be punished,
phrases.notes: "Punished" here means paying money for the lost babies.

phrases.english: if there is harm to the woman, they shall not be punished.
phrases.notes: "Harm" means the woman died. Then the verse says "life for life," so there is no money payment (שמות 21:23).

phrases.english: But not oxen:

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּיֵשׁ אָסוֹן, יֵעָנְשׁוּ.
phrases.english: for even though there is harm, they shall be punished.
Then the Torah wrote "the owner of the ox shall be clear":
that he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רבא's rejected answer with a new explanation of why רבי יוסי הגלילי needs 'בעל השור נקי'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reading of what 'men' excludes: the difference is about the case of אסון, not about תם and מועד.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since 'men' pay only when there is no אסון, oxen would be different and their owners would pay even when there is אסון.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'בעל השור נקי' teaches that the ox owner is exempt from דמי ולדות.

steps.title: רב אדא בר אהבה says it depends on intent, not on harm
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה challenges the new answer. Whether people pay or are exempt does not depend on whether the woman was harmed. It depends on whether they intended to strike her.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה objects: Does the matter depend on harm? The matter depends on intent!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה attacks the answer of אביי and רבא from Step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 assumed that the key question for people is whether there was אסון. רב אדא בר אהבה says that is the wrong question. What matters is the intent of the attacker. So the comparison to oxen based on אסון does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: He objects to it (introduces a challenge)
Is that to say...? (a challenging question)
Intent: what the person meant to do
The matter depends on...

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה:
phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects to this:
Is the matter dependent on harm?
The matter depends on intent!
phrases.notes: He means whether the attacker meant to hit the woman.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new answer of אביי and רבא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that people's liability for דמי ולדות depends on whether there was אסון.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Liability actually depends on the attacker's intent, not on whether the woman was harmed. So the contrast with oxen based on אסון falls apart.

steps.title: רב אדא בר אהבה explains why the ox owner is exempt from paying for the babies
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה says the deciding factor for people is intention. If they meant to hit each other, they pay for the babies even if the woman died. If they meant to hit her, they do not pay. Oxen would pay either way, so the פסוק 'בעל השור נקי' exempts them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אדא בר אהבה said: With people, when they meant to hit each other, they pay for the babies even if the woman died. When they meant to hit the woman herself, they do not pay. Oxen, though, would have paid even when they meant to hit the woman herself. So the תורה wrote 'בעל השור נקי' to teach that the ox owners are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה just rejected the earlier answer, and now he gives his own explanation of why we need the words 'בעל השור נקי'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For people, payment for the babies depends on whom they meant to hit. If they meant to hit the woman herself, they face the death penalty and so do not pay money. An ox owner never faces that death penalty, so we might have thought he always pays. The פסוק teaches that he is exempt from דמי ולדות.

keyTerms.meaning: they meant to hit each other
tragedy; here, the woman's death
they shall be punished, meaning here they pay money
the Merciful One, meaning the תורה
that they are exempt

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב אדא בר אהבה, people's liability for דמי ולדות depends on whom they meant to hit. 'בעל השור נקי' teaches that an ox owner is exempt from דמי ולדות.
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'not punished' does not mean the person got off easy. It means he does not pay money, because he is liable to the much more serious death penalty.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
Men: when they intended to strike each other,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב שֶׁיֵּשׁ אָסוֹן בָּאִשָּׁה, יֵעָנְשׁוּ;
phrases.english: even though there is a tragedy to the woman, they shall be punished (pay for the babies);

phrases.aramaic: כִּי נִתְכַּוְּנוּ לָאִשָּׁה עַצְמָהּ, לֹא יֵעָנְשׁוּ.
phrases.english: when they intended to strike the woman herself, they shall not be punished (pay).
phrases.notes: They don't pay money because they are liable to the death penalty for killing her.

phrases.english: But not so with oxen,
since even if they intended to strike the woman herself, 'they shall be punished.'
So the Merciful One wrote 'The owner of the ox shall be clear,' to teach that they are exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the answer of אביי and רבא in step 12, רב אדא בר אהבה offers his own explanation based on intention.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New explanation of why the פסוק is needed (a different starting assumption).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since an ox owner is never liable to death, he might have paid דמי ולדות even when the ox meant to hit the woman.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'בעל השור נקי' teaches that the ox owner is exempt from דמי ולדות.

steps.title: רב חגי brings a ברייתא that supports רב אדא בר אהבה
steps.stepSummary: When רב חגי came from the South, he brought a ברייתא that agrees with רב אדא בר אהבה's explanation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Likewise, when רב חגי came from the South, he brought with him a ברייתא that matches רב אדא בר אהבה's view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רב אדא בר אהבה by reporting that רב חגי brought a ברייתא from the South that says the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not quote the ברייתא here. It only reports that a תנאי source supports רב אדא בר אהבה. This gives his answer more weight than the answers that came before it.

keyTerms.meaning: from the South
he brought
a ברייתא (a teaching from the time of the תנאים)
in agreement with him

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן כִּי אֲתָא רַב חַגַּי מִדָּרוֹמָא,
phrases.english: And likewise, when Rav Chaggai came from the South,
he came and brought a baraita in his hand
in agreement with Rav Adda bar Ahava.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן כִּי אֲתָא רַב חַגַּי מִדָּרוֹמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a supporting ברייתא for the explanation given in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: רב אדא בר אהבה's explanation of 'בעל השור נקי'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that רב חגי brought from the South

steps.title: רבי עקיבא reads the verse as exempting the owner from paying for a slave
steps.stepSummary: A different ברייתא quotes רבי עקיבא, who says 'בעל השור נקי' means the owner is exempt from דמי עבד, the payment for a slave killed by the ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'The owner of the ox shall be clear.' רבי עקיבא says: clear from paying for the slave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new line of discussion by quoting another ברייתא with a completely different reading of 'בעל השור נקי'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the words 'בעל השור נקי' were explained in other ways, including רבי יוסי הגלילי's reading about דמי ולדות. רבי עקיבא says they are about the payment for a slave. This sets up the discussion that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: the payment owed for a slave killed by an ox

phrases.english: It is taught in another baraita:
'The owner of the ox shall be clear':

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: נָקִי מִדְּמֵי עֶבֶד.
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: clear from paying for the slave.
phrases.notes: This is the payment for a slave gored to death by an ox. See שמות 21:32.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the דמי ולדות discussion to a new תנאי reading of the same words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי עקיבא: 'בעל השור נקי' means the owner is exempt from דמי עבד.
